docs.source_name: Ante-Nicene Fathers, volume 4 (1885), via New Advent

docs.excerpt: Origen answers Celsus by pointing to Josephus: the Baptist's existence and his rite are reported by a writer who did not believe in Jesus, and who lived soon enough after the events to be a witness rather than a legend.

docs.title: Bethany beyond the Jordan (Al-Maghtas): the baptism site
docs.excerpt: Al-Maghtas, on the east bank of the Jordan in Jordan, is the principal traditional location of Jesus's baptism by John. It has been excavated as an archaeological site, not merely venerated as one.

docs.title: The Sozopol relics: what the AMS and DNA study actually reported
docs.excerpt: In 2010, excavation near the church of Saint John the Forerunner on Sveti Ivan island, off Sozopol in Bulgaria, produced a reliquary containing human and animal bones and a small inscribed box naming Saint John and his feast day.

docs.title: The "cave of John the Baptist" near Suba
docs.excerpt: In 2004 the archaeologist Shimon Gibson published a cave on Kibbutz Tzuba, west of Jerusalem, proposing it as a place John used. The identification is the most contested item in this collection.

docs.title: Machaerus: the fortress on the ridge
docs.excerpt: Machaerus is a Herodian palace-fortress on a ridge east of the Dead Sea, in present-day Jordan. Josephus places John's imprisonment and execution there, and the site is the one location in the story that archaeology can actually inspect.

docs.title: John and Qumran: a comparison, not an affiliation
docs.excerpt: The Essene-and-Qumran hypothesis is the most durable attempt to give John a setting. Wilderness, ritual purity, moral severity, scriptural interpretation and expectation of divine intervention all appear both in the Gospels' John and in the Dead Sea Scrolls. The question is what that overlap proves.

docs.title: Christian worship, art and liturgy
docs.excerpt: John's Christian afterlife is the largest of any figure in this archive except Jesus. It is not evidence about the first century; it is evidence about what communities did with him, and it is unusually well documented in institutions that can be checked.

docs.title: The Mandaeans
docs.excerpt: The Mandaeans are the only surviving religious community that treats John — in their own language, Yuhana — as a central figure on his own terms rather than as a forerunner to Jesus. They are also the hardest case in this archive to use as historical evidence, because the community's literature is l

docs.title: Yahya in Islam
docs.excerpt: In the Qur'an, John is Yahya, son of Zakariyya: a prophet in his own right, promised to an aged father, honoured as chaste and righteous, and given wisdom in childhood. Four surahs carry the material, and they are the primary record of the Islamic John.
